23.text: Visit to the Funeral Place. — On the second day after the funeral,

24.text: the relatives and friends of the dead one visit the corpse. This visit is

25.text: called “fetching of iron,” because most of the iron objects left with the

26.text: deceased are taken away, and replaced by wooden reproductions. Perhaps

27.text: this name has been devised in modern times, because, in conjunction with it,

28.text: the ceremony is also called “visiting the dead.” Besides fetching the iron,

29.text: one of its objects is to see whether beasts of prey have disturbed the

30.text: body. If this happens very soon, the relatives of the deceased feel secure.

31.text: On the contrary, any prolonged delay in the destruction of the body by beasts

32.text: signifies that the dead one is waiting for a companion. Another object of the

33.text: “visit” is to offer sacrifices, and to leave antlers with the dead.

34.text: The people who take part in “visiting the dead” are much more

35.text: numerous than the “followers” of the funeral procession. The inhabitants of

36.text: the camp, even the small children, go in a body; and guests come from a

37.text: circuit of fifty miles, especially if the deceased was a wealthy reindeer-breeder.

38.text: The herd, or a part of it, is brought along. Each of the visitors must bring

39.text: to the dead some little present, — a piece of sausage, some marrow from a

40.text: bone, a lump of sugar, a leaf of tobacco. The women of the camp prepare

41.text: and bring along quantities of sausage and meat-pudding, also all the marrow

42.text: from the reindeer slaughtered on the day of the funeral.
